entries.meaning: Words or drawings scratched or sprayed on a wall.
examples: Graffiti covers the whole underpass.
The city spends millions removing graffiti.
Political graffiti appeared overnight.
A Roman graffito on the wall names a gladiator.
The graffiti in the excavated house are mostly obscene.

senses.head: Wall writing, as a mass phenomenon
examples: Graffiti covers the whole underpass.
The city spends millions removing graffiti.
Political graffiti appeared overnight.

senses.head: A single inscription
examples: A Roman graffito on the wall names a gladiator.
The graffiti in the excavated house are mostly obscene.

entries.agreement: usually singular — graffiti is a problem here
entries.variants: the singular graffito survives only in archaeology and art history
entries.contrast: Strictly graffiti is plural and graffito singular. In practice English has made graffiti a mass noun taking a singular verb, and graffito sounds like a technical term. Both graffiti is everywhere and the graffiti are political can be defended; the first is far commoner.

entries.meaning: The speed at which music is played, or at which anything proceeds.
examples: The conductor took the second movement at a brisk tempo.
His tempi are famously fast.
Both tempos are marked in the score.
The tempo of the negotiations picked up.
She controls the tempo of the whole game.

senses.head: Musical speed
examples: The conductor took the second movement at a brisk tempo.
His tempi are famously fast.
Both tempos are marked in the score.

senses.head: The pace of any activity
examples: The tempo of the negotiations picked up.
She controls the tempo of the whole game.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the tempi vary between movements
entries.variants: tempos in general use; tempi among classical musicians
entries.contrast: Both are correct. Tempi signals a classical-music context; using it about a basketball game would sound strange.

entries.meaning: Someone with outstanding technical skill, especially in music.
examples: She was a virtuoso by the age of twelve.
Three virtuosos shared the stage.
The competition attracts virtuosi from every continent.
It was a virtuoso performance from start to finish.
His closing argument was a virtuoso piece of work.

senses.head: A highly skilled performer
examples: She was a virtuoso by the age of twelve.
Three virtuosos shared the stage.
The competition attracts virtuosi from every continent.

senses.head: Attributive — displaying great skill
examples: It was a virtuoso performance from start to finish.
His closing argument was a virtuoso piece of work.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the virtuosi were all under twenty
entries.variants: virtuosos is commoner in American English; virtuosi is used in classical criticism

entries.meaning: A freelance photographer who pursues celebrities.
examples: The paparazzi followed her car from the airport.
A single paparazzo waited by the stage door.
She has sued three paparazzi this year.
Paparazzi photographs sell for enormous sums.
The restaurant has a back entrance to avoid the paparazzi.

senses.head: The photographer
examples: The paparazzi followed her car from the airport.
A single paparazzo waited by the stage door.
She has sued three paparazzi this year.
Paparazzi photographs sell for enormous sums.
The restaurant has a back entrance to avoid the paparazzi.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the paparazzi were waiting outside
entries.variants: the singular paparazzo is rare; most speakers use paparazzi for any number
entries.contrast: Like graffiti, the plural has largely swallowed the singular. Strictly one photographer is a paparazzo, but ✗ a paparazzi is now very common in speech.

entries.meaning: An angelic being of the second order; in art, a chubby winged child.
examples: Two cherubim were carved above the ark.
The cherubim stand between heaven and earth.
The ceiling is covered in gold cherubs.
A stone cherub sits on each gatepost.
She was a perfect cherub until she turned three.

senses.head: A biblical angel
examples: Two cherubim were carved above the ark.
The cherubim stand between heaven and earth.

senses.head: A winged child in painting or sculpture
examples: The ceiling is covered in gold cherubs.
A stone cherub sits on each gatepost.

senses.head: A sweet-faced child
examples: She was a perfect cherub until she turned three.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the cherubim guard the ark
entries.variants: cherubim (angels of scripture) · cherubs (chubby winged children in art, or a sweet-looking child)
entries.contrast: ✗ Cherubims is a double plural — the -im is already the plural ending — though it appears in older translations of the Bible. The two plurals divide by register: solemn cherubim, everyday cherubs.

entries.meaning: An angelic being of the highest order.
examples: The seraphim have six wings each.
A single seraph stood before the throne.
Painters place seraphs at the top of the composition.
The hymn describes seraphim covering their faces.
Her expression was almost seraphic.

senses.head: The angel
examples: The seraphim have six wings each.
A single seraph stood before the throne.
Painters place seraphs at the top of the composition.
The hymn describes seraphim covering their faces.
Her expression was almost seraphic.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the seraphim sang
entries.variants: seraphim in scripture and poetry; seraphs in general use
entries.contrast: ✗ Seraphims is a double plural. The adjective is seraphic, meaning blissfully serene.

entries.meaning: A collective community in Israel, traditionally agricultural.
examples: He grew up on a kibbutz in the north.
Most kibbutzim have privatized since the 1990s.
The kibbutz runs a dairy and a guest house.
Several kibbutzim were founded by the same group.
Volunteers came from Europe to work on the kibbutz.

senses.head: The community
examples: He grew up on a kibbutz in the north.
Most kibbutzim have privatized since the 1990s.
The kibbutz runs a dairy and a guest house.
Several kibbutzim were founded by the same group.
Volunteers came from Europe to work on the kibbutz.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the kibbutzim were founded in the 1920s
entries.variants: kibbutzim is standard; kibbutzes occurs in casual English
entries.contrast: Note the stress shift: kih-BUUTS in the singular, kib-uut-SEEM in the plural, with the stress on the ending.

entries.meaning: A government department or news office; also a chest of drawers.
examples: The Federal Bureau of Investigation opened a case.
Both news bureaus were closed to save money.
She runs the paper's Tokyo bureau.
His keys were on top of the bureau.
They bought two matching bureaus.

senses.head: An office or agency
examples: The Federal Bureau of Investigation opened a case.
Both news bureaus were closed to save money.
She runs the paper's Tokyo bureau.

senses.head: A chest of drawers
examples: His keys were on top of the bureau.
They bought two matching bureaus.

entries.plural: bureaus — usual in American English · bureaux /ˈbjʊroʊz/
entries.agreement: plural verb — both bureaus reported the same figures
entries.variants: bureaus is standard American; bureaux is chiefly British
entries.contrast: The two plurals are pronounced identically — /ˈbjʊroʊz/ — so the choice is purely a spelling one. American style guides prefer bureaus.

entries.meaning: An area of level high ground; a period of no change after growth.
examples: The road climbs onto a high plateau.
These plateaus were carved by ancient rivers.
The plateau stretches for two hundred miles.
Sales have hit a plateau.
Learners often reach a plateau after the first year.
Both plateaus lasted about six months.

senses.head: A flat elevated landform
examples: The road climbs onto a high plateau.
These plateaus were carved by ancient rivers.
The plateau stretches for two hundred miles.

senses.head: A period of no further progress
examples: Sales have hit a plateau.
Learners often reach a plateau after the first year.
Both plateaus lasted about six months.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the plateaus rise sharply
entries.variants: plateaus is standard American; plateaux is chiefly British

entries.meaning: A striking arrangement of people or objects, as if in a picture.
examples: The pageant ended with a tableau of the founding.
Three tableaux were performed without a word.
The kitchen was a tableau of total disaster.
He described a tableau of families waiting in the rain.
Both tableaux stayed with me for years.

senses.head: A staged scene of motionless figures
examples: The pageant ended with a tableau of the founding.
Three tableaux were performed without a word.

senses.head: Any vivid scene
examples: The kitchen was a tableau of total disaster.
He described a tableau of families waiting in the rain.
Both tableaux stayed with me for years.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the tableaux were staged in silence
entries.variants: tableaux is commoner than tableaus, unlike bureaus and plateaus
entries.contrast: This is the one French plural in the group where the -x spelling still dominates in American English.

entries.meaning: An outline, plan, or underlying structure.
examples: The database schema changed in version three.
Both schemas need to be migrated.
He validates the file against a JSON schema.
Children build schemas to organize experience.
The schemata proposed by Kant are not empirical.

senses.head: A structural plan
examples: The database schema changed in version three.
Both schemas need to be migrated.
He validates the file against a JSON schema.

senses.head: A mental framework
examples: Children build schemas to organize experience.
The schemata proposed by Kant are not empirical.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the schemas were merged
entries.variants: schemas in computing and psychology; schemata in philosophy and formal scholarship
entries.contrast: Schemas is now overwhelmingly the commoner plural, especially in databases, where database schemas is the fixed phrase.

entries.meaning: A composition for solo instrument and orchestra.
examples: She recorded all five piano concertos.
Both concertos are in the same key.
The violin concerto runs forty minutes.
He has performed the concerti of Vivaldi.
A concerto needs a soloist; a symphony does not.

senses.head: The musical form
examples: She recorded all five piano concertos.
Both concertos are in the same key.
The violin concerto runs forty minutes.
He has performed the concerti of Vivaldi.
A concerto needs a soloist; a symphony does not.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both concertos are in D
entries.variants: concertos in general use; concerti among classical musicians
entries.contrast: Do not confuse a concerto — a work for soloist and orchestra — with a concert, the event where it is played.

entries.meaning: The text of an opera or musical.
examples: The libretto was rewritten twice.
Both librettos are printed in the program.
He wrote the libretto but not the music.
Several libretti survive without their scores.
A weak libretto can sink a fine score.

senses.head: The text
examples: The libretto was rewritten twice.
Both librettos are printed in the program.
He wrote the libretto but not the music.
Several libretti survive without their scores.
A weak libretto can sink a fine score.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both librettos were rewritten
entries.variants: both plurals are standard in music writing
entries.contrast: Italian for 'little book'. The libretto is the text; the score is the music.

entries.meaning: A distinguished conductor or musician; a master of any craft.
examples: The maestro took three curtain calls.
Both maestros refused to share the podium.
Several maestri studied under the same teacher.
He is the maestro of the backhand volley.
The pastry maestros worked through the night.

senses.head: A distinguished musician
examples: The maestro took three curtain calls.
Both maestros refused to share the podium.
Several maestri studied under the same teacher.

senses.head: A master of any craft
examples: He is the maestro of the backhand volley.
The pastry maestros worked through the night.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the maestros disagreed
entries.variants: maestros in general use

entries.meaning: The green summer squash.
examples: The zucchini in the garden are enormous.
Slice one zucchini lengthwise.
She grows more zucchinis than anyone can eat.
Grilled zucchini goes with everything.
Both zucchini had gone soft.

senses.head: The vegetable
examples: The zucchini in the garden are enormous.
Slice one zucchini lengthwise.
She grows more zucchinis than anyone can eat.
Grilled zucchini goes with everything.
Both zucchini had gone soft.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the zucchini are enormous
entries.pattern: Italian plural reanalyzed as a singular
entries.variants: American zucchini; British courgette
entries.contrast: In Italian zucchini is already plural — the singular is zucchino. English borrowed the plural, treats it as a singular, and then optionally adds -s. The same happened to panini, biscotti, and ravioli.

entries.meaning: A pressed grilled sandwich.
examples: He ordered a chicken panini.
Both paninis were burned on one side.
The café presses every panini to order.
Three paninis and two coffees, please.
In Italian, one of them is a panino.

senses.head: The sandwich
examples: He ordered a chicken panini.
Both paninis were burned on one side.
The café presses every panini to order.
Three paninis and two coffees, please.
In Italian, one of them is a panino.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the paninis are pressed to order
entries.pattern: Italian plural reanalyzed as a singular
entries.contrast: In Italian panini is the plural of panino, 'small bread roll'. American English treats panini as a singular and forms paninis, which is technically a double plural and completely standard.

entries.meaning: The hard twice-baked Italian cookie.
examples: The biscotti are meant for dipping.
She ate one biscotti with her coffee.
Both biscotti were almond.
He bakes biscotti every December.
In Italian, one of them is a biscotto.

senses.head: The cookie
examples: The biscotti are meant for dipping.
She ate one biscotti with her coffee.
Both biscotti were almond.
He bakes biscotti every December.
In Italian, one of them is a biscotto.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the biscotti are twice-baked
entries.pattern: Italian plural reanalyzed as a singular
entries.contrast: The Italian singular is biscotto. English speakers use biscotti for both numbers, exactly as with zucchini and panini.

entries.meaning: A woman's male admirer. Dated.
examples: She arrived with her latest beau.
All her former beaux were at the funeral.
Two beaus competed for her attention.
The word beau now sounds distinctly old-fashioned.
He was the most persistent of her beaux.

senses.head: The admirer
examples: She arrived with her latest beau.
All her former beaux were at the funeral.
Two beaus competed for her attention.
The word beau now sounds distinctly old-fashioned.
He was the most persistent of her beaux.

entries.plural: beaus — usual in American English · beaux /boʊz/
entries.agreement: plural verb — her beaux were all forgotten
entries.variants: beaus is the American spelling; beaux is the French one
entries.contrast: Both plurals are pronounced identically, /boʊz/ — the difference exists only on the page. The word is dated; modern American English says boyfriend.

entries.meaning: A French castle or large country house.

Several chateaux along the river are open to visitors.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the chateaux are open to visitors
entries.variants: also written château with the circumflex
entries.contrast: Identical in sound, different on the page — same as bureaus/bureaux. On wine labels Château names the estate.

entries.meaning: A social environment.
examples: He was never comfortable in that milieu.

The two milieus almost never mixed.
She writes about the artistic milieu of the 1920s.
Both milieux produced remarkable work.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the two milieus never mixed
entries.variants: milieus is commoner in American writing

entries.meaning: A large traveling bag; also a word blended from two others.
examples: He arrived with a battered leather portmanteau.

examples: He arrived with a battered leather portmanteau.
Both portmanteaus were monogrammed.

senses.head: A blended word
examples: Brunch is a portmanteau of breakfast and lunch.
The language is full of portmanteaux.
Several portmanteau words entered the dictionary that year.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the portmanteaus were monogrammed
entries.contrast: Best known now in portmanteau word — a word blended from two others, like brunch or smog — a use coined by Lewis Carroll.

entries.meaning: An arranged meeting.
examples: They arranged a rendezvous for midnight.

senses.head: The meeting
examples: They arranged a rendezvous for midnight.
Both rendezvous were canceled.
The rendezvous point was a parking garage.
Several rendezvous took place that week.
The spacecraft completed its rendezvous with the station.

entries.pronunciation note: the z and final s are silent
entries.plural: rendezvous /ˈrɑːndeɪvuːz/ — spelled the same, pronounced with a /z/
entries.agreement: plural verb — the rendezvous were arranged in advance
entries.contrast: Exactly like corps: the plural is distinguished only in sound. Singular ends in /uː/, plural in /uːz/.

entries.meaning: The frame of a vehicle or piece of equipment.
examples: The chassis is welded, not bolted.

senses.head: The frame

entries.plural: chassis /ˈʃæsiz/ — spelled the same, pronounced with a /z/
entries.agreement: plural verb — the chassis were welded
entries.contrast: Same shape as rendezvous and corps: singular /ˈʃæsi/, plural /ˈʃæsiz/, spelled identically.

entries.meaning: A very large ocean wave caused by an earthquake.
examples: The tsunami reached the coast in twenty minutes.

senses.head: The wave
examples: The tsunami reached the coast in twenty minutes.
Two tsunamis struck the same shoreline.
Tsunami warnings were issued across the Pacific.
A tsunami is not a tidal wave.

senses.head: An overwhelming surge
examples: A tsunami of complaints followed the announcement.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the tsunamis struck within minutes
entries.pattern: Japanese — no plural marking in the source language
entries.variants: English adds a regular -s; Japanese marks no plural at all
entries.contrast: Japanese loanwords take an English plural or none: tsunamis, samurai, ninja, sushi. The initial /ts/ cluster is hard for English speakers, who usually say soo-NAH-mee.

senses.head: The warrior
examples: The samurai were a hereditary class.
A single samurai guarded the gate.
Two samurai faced each other in the courtyard.
Samurai served a lord rather than a state.
The film follows seven samurai.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the samurai were a hereditary class
entries.variants: samurai is strongly preferred for the plural
entries.contrast: Like ninja, sushi, and manga, this stays unchanged. ✗ Samurais is not wrong but sounds naive.
